svg.text: THE OVERSELL — the bug we're preventing
unguarded: both read available = 5, both pass,
reserved becomes 6 — one customer gets no parcel
T3 is a DIFFERENT cell → different lock, no waiting
the contended unit is (sku, warehouse), nothing bigger
MUM-A has its own Entry.lock — fully parallel
Entry e = entries.computeIfAbsent(new Key(sku, wh), Entry::new)
reservations.put(id, new Reservation(id, sku, wh, qty))
READ + CHECK + WRITE in one critical section ⇒ check-then-act
is atomic. T2 sees available = 2 and is correctly rejected ✓
THE CELL, STEP BY STEP — onHand vs reserved
stock is still physically on the shelf — only promised
BOTH counters drop together, in one critical section — the parcel shipped
only reserved drops — nothing ever left the building
the invariant that holds at every row: 0 ≤ reserved ≤ onHand ✓
THE RESERVATION LIFECYCLE — and the order status that fires each verb
units go straight back to available; onHand never moved
release() and commit() both do reservations.remove(id) BEFORE taking the
lock. remove() is atomic, so exactly one caller gets a non-null Reservation;
everyone else sees null and throws "Unknown reservation".
the ConcurrentHashMap is doing idempotency work, not just lookup
The gap I'd name before the interviewer does:
a RESERVED reservation has no TTL. If the order service crashes between
reserve() and commit()/release(), those units are held forever —
available shrinks with no order to show for it.
Fix: an expiry timestamp + a sweeper that auto-releases — exactly the
hold-with-TTL pattern the airline seat design already uses.

g.text: always lock the smaller one first.
The snapshot is accurate the instant
it is taken and stale the instant it
race the lock exists to kill.
Let reserve() itself be the decision.

svg.text: ① draw the oversell race on one (sku, warehouse) cell → ② reserve() inside synchronized(e.lock) → ③ walk the onHand / reserved table row by row → ④ AVAILABLE → RESERVED → SHIPPED, with release() as the way back

g.text: ② Reserved units are never sold twice.
③ commit moves both counters atomically.
④ A reservation resolves exactly once.
